question: Which statement best describes Controlled vs uncontrolled?
options: By default, submitting an HTML form triggers a native browser submission that reloads the page, wiping out your React state. Calling e.preventDefault() in onSubmit cancels that behavior so you can handle the data in JavaScript instead. Always put it in the form's onSubmit handler rather than the button, since both Enter-key and button clicks fire onSubmit there.

Different controls report their value differently. Checkboxes use e.target.checked (a boolean) rather than e.target.value, while select, radio, and textarea all use value just like text inputs. Despite the differences they are all made controlled the same way — bind the relevant prop to state and update it in onChange. Forgetting to read checked instead of value on a checkbox is a common bug.

A controlled input derives its value from React state and updates that state on every change, so React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled input lets the DOM hold the value and you read it on demand through a ref. Controlled inputs unlock live validation and derived UI; uncontrolled inputs avoid per-keystroke re-renders and suit simple submit-only forms. The key gotcha is never mixing both on one input — don't pass value and defaultValue to the same field.

Rather than writing a separate setter for each field, store all fields in one state object and update it with a single handler keyed by the input's name attribute. This scales cleanly as forms grow and keeps the markup tidy. The crucial detail is using a computed property name ([name]) with the spread pattern so you update only the touched field and preserve the rest.

For large or complex forms, hand-rolled state and validation become repetitive and re-render heavy. Libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs under the hood and subscribe to fields individually, so typing in one field doesn't re-render the others. Paired with a schema validator like Zod or Yup, they make validation declarative and cut boilerplate dramatically. The tradeoff is an added dependency and a small learning curve.
